introduction-from-tables-to-graphs.core: Real applications have many-to-many relationships (users in groups, products in orders, people following people). Advanced DynamoDB modelling represents these graph-like relationships with key patterns (adjacency lists, inverted indexes), handles hot keys with sharding and builds filtered views with sparse indexes, all without joins.

first_principles.problem: A social app needs 'who follows me' and 'whom do I follow' at millions of QPS.
truths: Each direction needs its own access path.
derivation: **Invert keys** in a GSI for the reverse direction.

analogy.title: A city transit map
analogy.story: Stations are entities, lines are relationships, and you need to travel both directions.
analogy.breaks: Transit maps are fixed; social graphs change every second.

branches.label: Rule
children: Every access pattern has a key

example.title: Follow graph
flow: Query PK → following; query GSI1 → followers

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Both directions in one Query each.

check.q: How do you query both directions of a relationship in DynamoDB?
check.a: Store the edge with keys for one direction and add a GSI with inverted keys for the other.

adjacency-lists-the-schema-pattern.core: In the adjacency list pattern, each node and each edge is an item in the same table. The node's partition holds its metadata item plus one item per edge (SK = related entity), and an inverted GSI swaps PK/SK to traverse edges backwards. Edge items can carry attributes (role, joined date).

first_principles.problem: Modelling invoices ↔ bills (many-to-many) with separate tables requires app-side joins.

analogy.title: A contact book where each entry lists friends
analogy.story: Look up a person and see their friends; the reverse index shows who lists them.
analogy.breaks: Contact books are personal; DynamoDB edges must be kept consistent on both sides via the index.

check.q: What does the SK hold in an adjacency-list edge item?
check.a: The identifier of the related entity (e.g. USER#42).

write-sharding-solving-the-hot-partition.core: When one logical key gets more traffic than a partition can handle (a celebrity's follower list, a global counter, today's date), split it into N physical keys with a suffix. Random suffixes spread writes best but require reading all shards; calculated suffixes (hash of item ID) let you read one shard directly.

first_principles.problem: A celebrity's post gets 50,000 likes per second, all writing to PK=POST#1.
truths: Reads must know where to look.
derivation: Pick **N** from expected peak ÷ per-partition limit.

analogy.title: Splitting a long queue across numbered tills
analogy.story: Customers go to till number = last digit of their ticket, so staff know where to find any customer.
analogy.breaks: Tills are visible; shard counts are hidden in code and hard to change later.

code.text:
N = 50
def like(post_id):
    s = random.randrange(N)
    table.update_item(Key={'PK': f'POST#{post_id}#{s}', 'SK': 'LIKES'},
        UpdateExpression='ADD cnt :one', ExpressionAttributeValues={':one': 1})

def total(post_id):
    return sum(get(f'POST#{post_id}#{s}') for s in range(N))  # parallelise in practice

check.q: When should you use a calculated suffix instead of a random one?
check.a: When you need to read a specific item directly, since you can recompute its shard from its ID.

sparse-indexes-the-to-do-list-pattern.core: A GSI only contains items that have its key attributes. Setting an attribute (e.g. pending=true or GSI_OPEN=timestamp) only on items needing attention creates a sparse index, a cheap, small 'to-do list' that you query instead of scanning. Removing the attribute drops the item from the index.

first_principles.problem: Finding the 0.1% of orders awaiting review requires scanning millions of items.
truths: GSIs skip items missing the key.
Small indexes are cheap to query.
Attributes can be added and removed.
derivation: Add an **index attribute only when relevant**.
Shard the GSI PK if the list is **hot**.

analogy.title: Sticky notes on files that need attention
analogy.story: You look only at files with sticky notes, then peel them off when done.
analogy.breaks: Sticky notes fall off by accident; DynamoDB only removes the attribute when you do.

branches.label: Mechanism
children: GSI includes only items with key

example.title: Orders awaiting review
flow: Reviewers query GSI_REVIEW sorted by time

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Instant review queue over millions of orders.

check.a: Only items that have the GSI's key attributes appear in it.

putting-it-all-together-choosing-the-rig.core: Choose patterns from access needs: item collections for one-to-many, adjacency lists plus inverted GSIs for many-to-many, write sharding for hot keys, sparse indexes for filtered subsets, composite sort keys for hierarchical or time-range queries, and Streams for aggregates. Document every access pattern against the key or index that serves it.

first_principles.problem: Teams know individual patterns but combine them inconsistently.
truths: Each pattern solves a specific shape.

analogy.title: A carpenter's joinery techniques
analogy.story: Dovetail, mortise and tenon or dowel, each chosen for the joint in front of you.
analogy.breaks: Furniture is built once; access patterns evolve, so leave room for new GSIs.

check.q: Which pattern suits 'list only open support tickets'?
check.a: A sparse index populated only on open tickets.
